stops.note: a little bowl, diminutive of catinus; borrowed by Germanic peoples trading with Rome
Old English pronounced it with 'ch', like German Kessel
Viking settlers' ketill, also common as the name Ketil, gave English its hard k-
the electric kettle appeared in the 1890s, and the automatic switch-off came with Russell Hobbs in 1955

current_meaning: a container with a spout and lid for boiling water
